In the last two decades, a surge of interest has driven significant advancements in the field of Natural Language Processing, with deep neural networks emerging as the primary solution for various tasks, including the identification and extraction of relationships between entities in text. Due to limitations of traditional methods, researchers turned to alternative approaches, ultimately adopting deep neural networks for relation extraction tasks. A thorough analysis of existing literature reveals key techniques and future directions in this area, including the use of convolutional and recurrent neural networks for extracting meaningful features and utilizing attention-based models to prioritize essential information. Additionally, studies have explored the use of joint training and pre-trained networks for simultaneous feature extraction and relationship detection. As a result, notable improvements in relation extraction performance have been achieved.

This study investigates a Steklov-Robin characteristic value problem within a limited region in two dimensions. We demonstrate the following key points: (1) the existence and uniqueness of solutions can be guaranteed when certain conditions are met; (2) solutions can be efficiently calculated using the wavelet Galerkin method. The proposed method's wavelet basis does not need to meet an a priori compatibility condition. Moreover, our theoretical findings show that the convergence rate of solutions is directly related to the solution's overall smoothness. Finally, numerical experiments confirm the correctness of our conclusions.

We introduce a new hypergraph restoration method that utilizes a guide structure.
The guide structure, such as a skeleton tree, is integral to the graph's core structure and its weights significantly influence the weights of the surrounding edges.
Our approach identifies and optimizes the edges adjacent to the guide structure, and subsequently reconstructs the rest of the graph.
We demonstrate that our method successfully restores synthetic and natural datasets with missing values, and it has potential applications in analyzing neuronal connections, protein interactions, and more.

Radiologists can identify COVID-19 related abnormalities in patients' X-rays but it is difficult for radiology information systems to do so. A novel deep learning system was developed with a novel approach to generating radiologist-level annotations from CT scans, allowing CT-derived binary segmentation masks and binary classification to be projected onto patient X-rays. The resulting annotations align with radiologists' descriptions of COVID-19 related abnormalities detected on X-rays. The resulting annotation dataset consists of approximately 100,000 annotated images. This new dataset with rich understanding annotations enabled the training of a CT-free deep learning classifier for diagnosing COVID-19 based on patient X-rays. The performance of the classifier was comparable to that of an ensemble of radiologists. Research findings related to the new annotation dataset and method have been made available at https://github.com/epfml/COVID-XRay.

Euler characteristics of tight contact structures on specific types of three-dimensional manifolds have been calculated for an expanding class of these structures defined by a particular type of torus. It has been demonstrated that in many instances, the associated hypersurfaces are Heegaard surfaces, enabling a determination of their genera and consequently, using a known relationship between Foulkes-Thurston norms and Euler characteristics of tight contact structures, a Thurston norm calculation for these surfaces. This Thurston norm calculation then facilitates the identification of a particular cross-section of the dual to the Thurston norm. It has also been shown that an extension of this relationship to a broader class of contact structures, defined by a Heegaard surface, may not hold due to the non-convexity of the Thurston norm dual cross-section.

The introduction of non-linear optical micro-resonators enables the generation of a multitude of optical modes in a compact space. However, due to chaos arising from intricate coupling between these modes, stable operation of directional single-mode micro-cavity ring lasers becomes challenging. In this research, thermodynamic principles are applied to investigate the stability conditions of ring laser configurations with multiple modes. By extending the concept of specific entropy to systems with incompressible dynamics, our findings indicate that specific entropy decreases in steady states and directional outputs, but only increases during transient periods. The research demonstrates that maintaining a low entropy production rate is essential for the steady operation of directional outputs, especially when numerous modes are involved. To verify these theoretical conclusions, both numerical and experimental research on a silicon micro-cavity ring laser using an optical pump has been conducted, successfully showing a low entropy production rate for directional outputs and rejecting unstable multi-mode states like backward and 4-mode states, which exhibit high entropy production rates.

This study examines the price changes of cryptocurrencies used for transaction purposes, focusing on their average daily price variations. We found that these changes follow an exponential distribution, which is consistent with Smoluchowski's model of consistent evolution. This indicates that the price changes are largely unaffected by market speculation. In contrast, we analyzed the prices of cryptocurrencies that serve as stores of value, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum Classic, Bitcoin Cash, Monacoin, and Dash. These price changes also follow an exponential distribution but with significantly higher inconsistency factors. Additionally, we investigated the relationship between a cryptocurrency's supply and its market capitalization, and we compared the characteristics of cryptocurrencies used for exchange with those that serve as a store of value. Our analysis revealed differences in supply elasticity and price stability between these two groups, which may have implications for their use as a medium of exchange or as a store of value.

The KPZ equation, which models a wide range of phenomena, is accompanied by a faint noise theory, characterized by a log-correlated landscape, while its square, representing a strongly disordered environment, is itself theoretically plausible. However, a connection between these two regimes, transitioning from weak to strong noise, is absent. We utilized the inverse scattering method associated with the Riemann-Hilbert problem to develop a new approach, enabling the construction of strong noise solutions based on an analysis of a specific operator's properties. Based on these properties, we developed an algorithm to construct Wiener-Hopf factorizations, ultimately leading to the creation of both weak and strong noise solutions. Our theory unifies these two regimes, providing a rare connection between the two extremes.

MMS data from the solar wind have primarily focused on turbulent structures larger than 1000 km. A smaller-scale analysis of compressive turbulence, detected by the MMS team using plasma and electromagnetic data, has provided essential insights into the dissipation process of turbulent energy. This study employs machine learning to investigate the MMS observations of compressive turbulence and determines the scale at which electron dissipation occurs. The scale of these turbulent events was estimated using the Volden scale analysis, revealing that they reached down to the electron diffusive scale of 100s of meters.

High-intense, attosecond-duration pulses in the extreme ultraviolet to soft X-ray spectrum can be generated using a Strong-Field High Harmonics process seeded in a powerful external laser source, when integrated into an existing Free-Electron Laser facility. When seeded at the European XFEL, this technique yields yields as high as 10 in the 100-angstrom range, although the generated pulses typically measure around 150 attoseconds in duration. By implementing a novel electron bunch modification method, specifically a modified chirp-taper approach, it is possible to reduce the pulse duration to below 50 attoseconds. The proposed electron modification technique involves optimally tailoring the electron bunch profile and its associated current distribution to enhance the produced harmonics' intensity and coherence, despite the varying gain characteristics across the electron bunch. Optimal conditions result in yields nearing 1 and pulse durations around 50 attoseconds.

Our research introduces a new method for calculating the long-term behavior of shear flows in complex, layered fluids with varying viscosity levels. We demonstrate that this behavior can be accurately modeled using an optical approach, which also allows us to derive closed-form equations for key current patterns. In addition, we develop a precise formula for the magnitude of shears within the flow, yielding a solution that matches existing theoretical models by Carson-Hinch, particularly in the case of specific viscosity ratios.

Our research introduces a marking process that takes as input two parameters: the probability of a vertical or horizontal split, denoted as $p$, and a value for the maximum allowable discrepancy between parties' vote counts, den as $\delta$. The marking process generates an instance of this scheme by dividing the electoral map into equal-sized regions and assigning each voter a party affiliation, ensuring that the resulting map meets the constraint on vote count discrepancy. The resulting marked map is then used to calculate the gerrymandering index, which measures the effectiveness of the marking process in creating balanced regions. The effectiveness of this marking process is demonstrated by its ability to produce marked maps with an average gerrymandering index within a logarithmic factor of the optimal possible value. Furthermore, our research provides a guaranteed upper bound on the mixing time of a modified version of this marking process when used as a dynamic electoral system, which is determined by the choice of $p$ and $\delta$ parameters.

The inspection of patterned textile products like floral patterns is challenging due to the similarity between the design elements. Traditional inspection methods are ineffective for these products, so a more advanced approach is needed. To address this, this research presents a novel technique based on the maximization of image differences to identify anomalies in patterned textile images. Initially, the primary design pattern is extracted using a maximum difference-based image difference maximization (MDIDAM) approach, then decomposed into a consistent background pattern and random noise using a low-rank decomposition method. The MDIDAM method calculates difference maps for various potential pattern positions and selects the one corresponding to the design pattern based on a mean absolute error metric, before decomposing the chosen pattern. The proposed method was tested on a dataset of common textile flaws and achieved a classification accuracy of 94% through the calculation of a classification score using the KNN algorithm, demonstrating a significant improvement over existing methods.

A key challenge in fully autonomous systems is navigation, which can be addressed by combining deep reinforcement learning and visual cues. However, a significant hurdle in this approach is the instability of policy updates. We introduce a novel system, Data-Theoretic Policy Regularization, which applies an information-theoretic principle to improve policy updates by maintaining the distribution of reward sequences. Extensive tests on real-world navigation datasets and various challenges demonstrate that our method achieves significant performance gains, particularly in navigating unfamiliar environments without prior knowledge.

As a direct mass absorber, the black hole black hole (BH-BH) system experiences mass accumulation through the Bondi process, primarily when passing through the interstellar medium (ISM). This mass accumulation alters the orbital dynamics of the BH-BH system, influencing its long-term evolution. Although mass accumulation has been shown to have significant effects on BH binaries, its mass accumulation rate has never been constrained observationally. This study aims to establish an upper limit on the Bondi mass accumulation rate by analyzing BH mass measurements from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and standard cosmological models, which determine BH mass distributions. By modeling the bondi mass accumulation process, the EHT's precision in measuring BH masses sets a pace on mass accumulation rates for supermassive BHs. This research provides a fundamental constraint that future BH mass measurements will utilize to further investigate BH mass evolution in various cosmological contexts.

Deep within dense galactic centers lie clusters of young stars known as Nuclear Star Clusters (NSCs), characterized by extremely high star densities. Through complex interactions, these clusters evolve, resulting in the formation of massive black holes (MBHs) that eventually merge into a single central supermassive black hole (SMBH) surrounded by a few MBHs. Simultaneously, lower-mass stars continue to form through interactions, generating gravitational waves. Research indicates that these waves could surpass the sensitivity limits of the LIGO detector, offering a unique window into the early life of these galactic regions.

In modern smart distribution grids with smart meters, detecting distinct occurrences like outages, restorations, and scheduled events is becoming a feasible task. This capability can be leveraged for enhanced service, including improved fault diagnosis, accurate state estimation, and real-time fault detection, tracing, and quantification. This chapter outlines a practical approach for extracting all events from active power flow data collected at a subset of feeders. This method relies on a data-driven analysis of power trends and an accompanying algorithm to standardize and categorize the detected events according to predefined criteria.

The properties of the X(3872) are investigated experimentally by analyzing its interactions with a photon and two-photon interactions with a $J/\psi$ meson. 
A theoretical framework is employed to calculate transition amplitudes for the decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3372)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \delta$. 
Key considerations include wave function overlap and radiative width. 
Computed results are compared to available experimental data. 
Findings suggest that the electric quadrupole and weak magnetic moments of the X(3872) are approximately $-0.44(2)$ and $0.62(2)$ times the decay constant of a $\rho$ meson. 
Additionally, the two-photon decay width of X(3872) is estimated at $1.25(10)$ eV.

We define specific categories - known as category of quadrics, as subcategories within derived categories of smooth projective varieties, by identifying unique characteristics. These characteristics include a characteristic polynomial for the spherical object in the category, which always equals $t^4-2t^3-t$. The existence of a tri-equivalence between the n-cube of the quadric category and the derived category of a localizing subcategory in the n-fold derived tensor product category is established under certain conditions, particularly when char$k$ does not divide $2^n(n+1)$. The solution to a long-standing problem by Knudsen and Mumford is obtained as a consequence of this discovery, which provides a new proof that spherically fused objects in the quadric category, in the given condition, form a simple vector space.

A recent breakthrough in AI research focuses on mastering general AI abilities within virtual environments, but a significant limitation exists within the study domain due to slow environment interaction rates, typically around three to fifty million interactions per hour. To overcome this constraint and accelerate the learning process, a new high-speed emulator called TextWorldExpress is presented. By effectively simulating over one million interactions per second, TextWorldExpress achieves a significant environment simulation speedup while maintaining realistic learning conditions. As a direct consequence of this high-speed capability, a state-of-the-art language-based AI model, FAST, is now able to master all three of the text-based game challenges within the textAI benchmark within just two days. Furthermore, the TextWorldExpress emulator enables FAST to outperform previous approaches that simulated individual AI interactions in real-time by a substantial margin, demonstrating a notable improvement of up to three orders of magnitude.

To establish the bulk-boundary correspondence in dimension $d$, a geometric approach requires specific conditions: smoothness and periodicity of the geometric framework, both of which are compromised when an insulator has defects. In order to satisfy these conditions, we propose using a smooth and periodic model to represent an insulating system with defects. This approach involves embedding the insulating system into a larger, smooth and periodic framework and demonstrating that it effectively reproduces the properties of the defective system. Further, we identify and study 'flux insertions' as a means of characterizing insulating systems, which allow for the characterization even when a system has a finite energy gap but no topological protection. In order to maintain smoothness and periodicity, we must introduce compensating electrons or holes, leading to 'gapless edge states' that circumnavigate isolated defects while passing through a sea of defects in dimension $d$. Our approach successfully recovers and generalizes key topological invariants, including the Chern number, winding number, and topological Hall conductivity, even in multi-band scenarios.

Harnack's inequality for p harmonic functions is examined within the context of a sector-shaped domain, with assessments of Harnack inequalities derived in terms of the sector's dimensions and a function specific to boundary arc lengths. This function is subsequently bounded in terms of the sector's dimensions, with certain cases considered in detail. These calculations facilitate the analysis of heat diffusion through a thin wedge.

Using a well-known extreme environment map, researchers can calculate the univariate conditional extreme probabilities for each station, given the data from surrounding stations, and identify the most dangerous areas. However, this does not provide the answer to the question of how many times such an environment could be experienced in the future, and we aim to address this gap by considering the multivariate approach. By assuming station independence, we can calculate the conditional extreme probabilities for each station, but this does not reflect the real-world connection between stations, and we aim to address this limitation using a novel method based on the extreme multivariate spatial model. By applying the approach to the analysis of storms affecting France, our results show that taking into account the connection between stations leads to an increase in the estimated occurrence of extreme events, and we can identify areas with the highest risk, which may change depending on the surrounding stations' data.

Let $k$ be a fixed algebraic number field and $f,\:g$ two polynomials not belonging to the set of constant functions with coefficients in $k$. We denote the roots of the equation $k$ as $P$ and $Q$, both also non-constant with coefficients in $k$. Let the heights of $P$ and $Q$ be denoted as $H(P)$ and $H(Q)$, respectively, and let $d$ be the degree of the function field $k$. Then, there exist constants $C_1$ and $C_2$, dependent only on $k$, such that the following inequality is true:
$$
\max\{ \lambda_{\mathbf{P}^{1}}(P), \lambda_{\mathbf{P}^{1}}(Q) \} \leq \frac{d+1}{4} \log H(d) + C_1,
$$
where $\lambda_{\mathbf{P}^{1}}$ represents the relative canonical height on the projective line defined over $k$.

A recently developed concept called human-to-robot manipulability realm adjustment addresses the limitations of traditional robot manipulation by increasing its flexibility and adaptability when working alongside humans. However, achieving this of MRRA has proven difficult due to the complexity of accurately positioning the robot in sync with the human. To overcome these challenges, a new parallel planning strategy is proposed that incorporates an improved iterative closest point algorithm with surface awareness to facilitate smooth and accurate MRRA.

A primary goal of the Heavy Ion and Tyrecker Group at Fermilab is to thoroughly analyze Higgs boson pair production, and we have developed a novel approach using matrix element techniques to study the 2-body Higgs boson pair creation via the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\textrm{b}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel. Additionally, we have designed an innovative method to efficiently calculate the differential cross-section of this process. Our study focuses on the study of Higgs boson pair production via the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\textrm{b}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel for center-of-mass energies of 13 and 14 TeV. We also present a comparison between matrix element and fixed-order next-to-leading order results, and propose potential observables for experimental investigations of Higgs boson pair creation.

Our research focuses on how an agent can learn to locate objects in a 3D environment when the only changes are the rotations of those objects. To achieve this, we developed a new type of network that can be adapted to any 3D scene and has the potential to replicate the brain's processing of spatial information. By assuming the scene can be broken down into separate parts, we found the network self-organizes into two distinct brain-like areas: one that encodes the position of objects and another that encodes their rotation. This results in an area that can understand the layout of the scene and another that can recognize the orientation of objects. This finding provides insight into how the brain might process spatial information and opens up the possibility of applying what we learned to more complex scenes with moving objects.

A growing concern on social media platforms is the spread of false COVID-19 vaccine information, which can lead to negative public health outcomes. To address this problem, we have developed a dataset consisting of Twitter conversations between pro and anti-vaccine users. Our task is to accurately identify the pro or anti-vaccine user's stance within a conversation by examining their posts. Our experiments using this dataset confirm the effectiveness of a Language Model in distinguishing and tracking conversations, surpassing traditional text classification models by a significant margin (11.12% improvement). Our code and data can be accessed at the provided link.

A two-step process is proposed to generate isolated attosecond pulses with higher energy and efficiency, utilizing a high-intensity, short-duration electric field from a plasma source. By first creating a plasma sheet through intense laser interaction with a gas target and then applying a short-interval high-intensity field, the proposed method yields more compact and powerful attosecond pulses. A simulation demonstrates the possibility of producing multiple short pulses, which can be combined into isolated attosecond pulses with significantly increased yield, occurring every 2 periods of the driving electric field.

Recent observations by Gaia and other sources have identified potential companions associated with variable star systems of the Algol type. Although many of these candidates were initially dismissed due to inconsistencies in photometric data, the companion within HD37112 has not been as readily dismissed. Utilizing light curve and radial velocity data, including that from the APASS, ZTF, NGTS, and GTC/OSCAR telescopes, researchers examined possible gaia20agk signals. Unlike previous studies, this examination did not yield evidence of a signal suppressing the companion's presence. Instead, the data supports an eccentric orbit, yielding an estimated eccentricity of 0.61 plus or minus 0.08. Although not yet confirmed, HD37112 continues to be among a select group of systems warranting closer scrutiny.

Consider a time-dependent, complex-valued function $u(t,x)$ defined for $t>0$ within a given bounded domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb R^N$. Its behavior is governed by a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a positive parameter $\alpha<\frac{2\pi}{T}$, a nonlinear term involving a parameter $p$, and a Dirichlet boundary condition outside the domain $\Omega$. Our research reveals the nonexistence of certain explosive solutions, under a certain convexity condition, in the case of unbounded domains, but not necessarily in the case of bounded domains. Our results extend the work of several researchers, including Fong, Li and Zhang in the bounded domain case, and several researchers, including Fong, Li and Zhang in the unbounded case, to the situation where the domain $\Omega$ has a more complex boundary. Our new boundary condition is given in a straightforward form, and encompasses several previously established conditions, including those of Li and Zhang in the bounded and unbounded cases.

Physically-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer an innovative solution to partial differential equations, incorporating physical laws into a flexible, data-driven framework that doesn't require a grid. However, PINNs struggle with problems involving multiple scales and unknown boundary conditions. This paper introduces Residual-driven Adaptive Node Generation, or RANG, a method that dynamically adds data points where the model's accuracy is lowest and creates virtual boundaries based on the problem's scale. Through testing with two problems of different scales, RANG has been shown to outperform traditional training methods, even when the model's parameters are adjusted to account for several orders of magnitude in input output values.

The combination of ferroelectric and semiconductor technologies has the potential to overcome their individual limitations, making them suitable for next-generation logic and memory applications. A novel nonvolatile transistor called a ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET) has emerged as a promising solution. FeFETs utilize a crucial property known as negative capacitance (NC) to effectively switch between a low-power off-state and a robust on-state. Recent breakthroughs in growing multicomponent ferroelectric films have led to improvements in their electrical characteristics and their incorporation into FeFETs. However, the behavior of these films in horizontal devices has not been fully understood. A computational model that accounts for the complexities of multidomain ferroelectric films is essential for their design. This film system features a stable, thin grounded layer on a dielectric substrate and can be charged by applying a voltage. The simulation shows that a moving domain wall can create an electrostatic potential that causes the semiconductor channel to switch between a weak on-state and a strong on-state. The model indicates that negative capacitance can be controlled by adjusting various factors, such as dielectric thickness and semiconductor doping levels. The accuracy of this computational model can be verified against recent experimental findings.

A major disruption to the U.S. freight transport network has the potential to cause widespread ripple effects due to the interconnected nature of industries and units within it. 
To better comprehend and forecast dependency and fragility in the freight transport system, this study develops an information graph using user-supplied data. 
By employing an unit failure function, the method evaluates the U.S. freight system's vulnerability, taking into account both direct and indirect losses. 
Using a user-friendly interface, the research enables users to identify key areas of dependency and fragility within the system and has been applied to the U.S. freight system to demonstrate utility. 
Further, an information-based metric is proposed for measuring system fragility, which is used to develop an index for ranking areas of the U.S. freight system in terms of fragility. 
The research also discusses user considerations when applying the proposed approach.

This study investigates the irreducibility of stochastic intricate Ginzburg-Landau equations subject to discontinuous disturbances. To establish a precise criterion for irreducibility, we first derived a stochastic normal form for these equations and then applied a strong attractivity criterion to equations with mixed disturbances. Combining the techniques of a small set condition and Freidlin--Khasminskii's theorem from large deviation theory, we proven a large deviation result. Furthermore, the notion of irreducibility for a class of intricate systems with pure jump disturbances is then generalized.

Given a finite group G, the set of non-generator elements is defined, where it includes every element whose order is a prime power. For a group G, the chromatic number of its power graph, denoted χ(℘(G)), is equal to the maximum chromatic numbers of the subgraphs made up of elements with a specific prime base. In the case of a nilpotent group, we identify a minimum value for this maximum chromatic number. Furthermore, for groups G and H, an equivalence is established based on this minimum value. Similar findings were initially explored by some researchers.

A high-tech fast hadron detector called HFADG has been designed to operate within the LHC's collision zone with remarkable precision, capable of detecting individual particles even at high collision rates of up to 75 TeV. This innovative system utilizes advanced technologies such as time-of-flight flight times, a TOF microphone, and a tof camera. Furthermore, research using simulations has been conducted to determine the capability of the HFADG in measuring the LHC's central particle density and distinguishing between jets of different jets. In addition to its potential for use at the LHC, the HFADG can also be used to study fast cosmic radiation in both terrestrial and airborne environments.

This study builds upon the success of non-strictly shift-equivariant image feature detectors by integrating the concepts of geometric non-strict shift-equivariance and geometric convolutional networks. By combining these ideas, we demonstrate the feasibility of creating practical and efficient orientation convolutional networks for image recognition, which are both computationally efficient and analytically manageable. Furthermore, these new concepts can be extended to handle images with rotational symmetry and generate comprehensive orientation fields, providing valuable insights into image recognition beyond traditional methods.

Recent advancements in learning frameworks have enabled researchers to develop
more precise and intelligent computer vision and vision-free systems.
However, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) face accuracy limitations when
applied to unstructured 3D data like raw point clouds. To address these
limitations, our study proposes novel extensions to GCNs that enhance their
capacity to process point clouds by introducing new layers and operations.
The proposed extensions include introducing max-pooling layers and a novel operation
that merges multiple neighboring points into a single aggregated neighboring point.
Additionally, we develop new methods for normalizing point clouds to improve their
geometric features. Our proposed enhancements are validated on three public datasets
for 3D classification and point-based segmentation, demonstrating their
effectiveness in boosting the performance of GCNs on such datasets.

We've discovered that conventional Trojan detection methods using JSON-based semantic frameworks are ineffective in identifying hostless Trojans (HTs), a type of malware commonly distributed through Microsoft Store and Google Play Store mobile applications. The reason for this shortcoming lies in the developers' ability to mask HTs by removing semantic JSON nodes that contain sensitive mobile API calls, leaving only the high-level semantic framework intact - a tactic that evades traditional Trojan detection methods. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel hostless Trojan detection method, called AST-SAN, which employs machine learning to analyze the dynamic behavior of HTs and identify patterns that are absent in their sanitized versions. The results from our experiments using a dataset of 10,000 Microsoft Store and Google Play Store applications demonstrate that the SAN framework alone provides no value in HT detection, while the effectiveness of our proposed method is significantly improved when combined with an 80% attention ratio for positive samples and a 60% for negative samples - achieving an AUC score of 0.9025 and 0.8688, respectively, outperforming existing mobile API call-based state-of-the-art techniques.

We present recent developments and updated performance characteristics of the ROSIE integral field unit integrated into the Magellan IMACS spectrometer. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the ROSIE's optical design, guiding detector, and data processing methods. By utilizing a grid of 648 optical fibers with a 2.5 arcsec pitch, the ROSIE's 3x3 pixel CCD camera captures a 2D spectral view. Each fiber's contents are analyzed through an optimized cross-dispersion system employing a custom rosette grating and a 3kx2k E2V CCD. As a result, 3D volumes spanning 1.08 deg^2 are captured at 1.25 arcsec spatial and 1.5 Angstrom spectral resolutions across a wavelength range of 390-960 nm using three distinct detector modes. We discuss the performance of IMACS+ROSIE in point source and extended object imaging, supported by recent observations demonstrating the system's scientific potential.

In this paper, a comprehensive status report on deep subbarrier fusion for the collision of two carbon-12 nuclei is presented, with a focus on enhancing the technique known as the Trojan horse method.

This research focuses on predicting the mass, radius, and density of hypothetical terrestrial planets around certain stars observed by the CHEOPS and TESS missions. A Bayesian statistical method is employed to estimate the mass of these planets based on their stars' compositions. A sample of 17 Earth-like planets and their corresponding host stars were selected, using existing data on masses, radii, and chemical abundances. The results indicate a measured average Earth planet mass of 0.833 M⊕ and radius of 0.942 R⊕. Factors such as iron and silicon abundance, as well as magnesium, significantly influence the mass of these planets. Moreover, the model accounts for metal depletion in gas giant stars, suggesting that their terrestrial planets may be smaller than expected. The model also considers the variation in mantle iron content. The predicted masses are generally within 20% of the actual masses, while predicted radii may deviate by up to 20%. These predictions align with the masses and radii of hypothetical planets similar to GJ 1238 b.

Current wireless localization is limited by signal attenuation, leading to significant positioning errors at millimeter wave frequencies. In order to mitigate this issue and reduce location uncertainty, we propose an innovative approach based on deep learning that utilizes channel state information. By focusing on the most relevant features of the channel, our method filters out noise and channel variations in order to enhance the target object's signal. As a result, our system demonstrates millimeter-level accuracy in a real-world environment with a significant reduction in the impact of distance and noise on the position of the target object.

This paper treats modality as a fundamental grammatical element and develops modal logic from basic principles, similar to how type theory is approached in natural approaches to the philosophy of science. By integrating multiple systems of reasoning, the method offers benefits such as a clear model of meaning, effective decision procedures, and constructive proofs. The decision procedures utilized in this research are adapted from existing solutions, such as those developed for union types, almost difference types, and spatial reasoning systems. The paper also features an original approach to the completeness theorem, which can be visualized as a modal compactness result.

A bipartite graph's edges can be altered to a star pattern within each part of the vertex set, subject to constraints, to meet the valence requirements, known as the Edge Star Transformation problem, which has been studied in the context of the 3d-Edge Star Transformation for 3-regular bipartite graphs. A previously claimed proof stating such transformations are always possible for 3-regular bipartite graphs is now found to be erroneous, along with the related conjecture that such transformations are always feasible for trees with 3 leaves. An example graph showing the failure of this conjecture is presented along with an alternate proof that such transformations are feasible for certain classes of bipartite graphs.

By examining the Hamming graph H(n, q), this research finds the minimum possible support size of a function with a spectrally constrained range, specifically where the non-zero elements of the function's vector are limited to the highest (k+1) eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix. Leveraging the structure of the Hamming graph, the study demonstrates the existence of a function with a minimum support size of k + 1 within the given spectral constraints. Furthermore, under certain conditions regarding n, k, and q, it's proven that the minimum support size is exactly k + 1. These results are derived through the application of an inductive argument and the development of a recursive relationship between the adjacency matrix's eigenvalues, which also provides an alternative method to establish Slepian's result.

COPASI is a comprehensive investigative tool for mathematical modeling of complex systems in biology and physics, featuring an integrated graphical interface that enables users to interact with models through an array of functionality, from basic simulations to advanced Bayesian inference. However, with its extensive capabilities, navigating COPASI's command-line operations can be daunting, particularly when performing tasks repeatedly or learning the model's underlying mathematics. To address this limitation, a new web-based platform, ShinyCOPASI, has been developed, allowing users to interact with COPASI models through a seamless web interface, facilitating enhanced investigation of dynamic systems, as showcased through several practical examples.

A new intelligence for scientific applications is gaining prominence, and ambiguity measurement is becoming a key focus for assessing its key limitations. This course introduces AMI, a subset of interpretability within reliability, and explores its evaluations within a broader context of scientific machine intelligence. We examine multiple methods for measuring ambiguity, including entropy and other intrinsic techniques, as well as extrinsic evaluation methods that utilize pointouts and inputs. We also cover various approaches for evaluating AMI, such as extrinsic and intrinsic evaluations, and highlight challenges and potential breakthroughs in AMI for multiple scientific domains, including physics, medicine, and botany.

This article investigates a specific von Neumann algebra generated by a compact quantum group's category functions within the category functions operator algebra. The study reveals that this von Neumann algebra always has a separable property. Furthermore, the article establishes the condition under which the category functions operator algebra and the generated von Neumann algebra are identical. In addition, the article proves that the category functions operator algebra has a finite dimensionality if and only if the quantum group is a finite group. Ultimately, the article provides certain calculations and dimensions for specific examples of non-commutative compact quantum groups.

This study introduces a modified strategy iteration method with tolerances that can work efficiently on large systems of linear equations representing Markov decision processes (MDPs) with many states. The method involves two steps: initially, a rough solution is found through power iteration, followed by using strategy iteration with set-inclusive order relations to refine it. By making the order relations imprecise, the method reduces computational complexity from linear to constant time per element. The study presents a theory and numerical tests showing the enhanced strategy iteration strategy converges faster than traditional strategy iteration when using set-inclusive order relations.

In a significantly larger body of research compared to my contribution, edge ideals of hypergraphs have been examined due to their edge ideal of graph equivalents being well-understood. This post aims to provide an extensive analysis similar to that found in other studies, but specifically for the weighted directed graphs case. Specifically, for weighted directed graphs, I present formulas for the general symbolic and regular homological dimensions as well as determining the conditions under which these dimensions reach their maximum or minimum values. Furthermore, I will define and investigate the property of being an s-star common to these graphs and will establish both the conditions for being a maximal instance of this property as well as defining and defining the maximum number of such instances possible within any given weighted directed graph.

High-fidelity computer simulations provide valuable insights into complex systems across various fields. The accuracy of these models, however, can be compromised by uncertainties in input parameters. To address this, randomized simulations are employed to evaluate the impact of uncertainties on model output. The resulting output distributions are analyzed at specific points in time, often requiring intricate integrals over a multi-dimensional space. This analysis is further complicated when dealing with time-series data, as it necessitates sophisticated numerical methods. The paper tackles this analytical challenge by introducing an efficient method to calculate time-dependent uncertainty across multiple instances of the same simulation at different times. The effectiveness of this method is illustrated through a series of 3D incompressible flow simulations, where a statistical inference technique is applied to determine the most likely vortices shedding frequency in a flow past a cylinder, based on time-series data from three distinct Reynolds numbers. The proposed algorithm demonstrates a significant reduction in computational cost, with nearly a 1000-fold decrease in the number of required evaluations for forward simulations.

This study investigates Residual Connection Regionalization (RCR), a technique for robust learning from regionally partitioned data under partially corrupted labels, applicable to both classification and regression tasks. RCR pairs each region with a global network, allowing them to interact through RCR. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RCR when using a local learning approach, particularly when regional data distributions significantly diverge from the global distribution. Additionally, we developed a novel loss function, the Local Global Discrepancy Loss (LGDL), to quantify the variation between global and regional losses in order to strike a balance between model resilience and accuracy. Using LGDL, we can tune the model's resilience based on the level of data heterogeneity, and our model outperforms existing methods on datasets such as MNIST variants, CIFAR10, and Neuromorphous datasets.

The reconstruction of isolated-photon-tagged jets in Pb-Pb collisions, specifically with a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.02 TeV, is investigated in this study. By comparing these measurements to those from proton-proton collisions, effects of the underlying event and energy loss are evaluated and accounted for. Using CMS detector data collected during 2016, results are obtained for cross-sections involving isolated-photon-tagged jets with specific transverse momentum and rapidity ranges. After correcting for energy loss and other factors, differences in fragmentation functions between Pb-Pb and proton-proton collisions are determined and show that in Pb-Pb collisions, there is an overall decrease in the energy carried by particles produced within jets, particularly in Pb-Pb collisions at the lower pn threshold.

Recent research has provided novel identities rooted in hypergeometric functions that allow the calculation of infinite series related to Riemann zeta functions and multiple zeta values through non-analytic components such as floor functions and parity-based terms. Building upon recent findings, we will now present more general identities of a similar nature in this paper to derive complex expressions including colored multiple zeta expressions and quasicrystals. Our approach will enable the computation of infinite series with alternating or non-alternating terms as the summation index changes, based on non-analytic terms. The resulting identities will facilitate the calculation of deep quadratic Gauss sums and quasi-beta expressions.

Recent observations of the brown dwarf system WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 by the JWST have shed new light on it. The object, previously known as "2MAJ153429.7-104303.4" and nicknamed "Mishap" due to conflicting age estimates, has been the subject of controversy. High-resolution spectroscopy obtained by the NIRSpec on the JWST has enabled a more accurate determination of its properties, including surface gravity, which suggests a much younger age of around 30 million years, in line with other estimates. This discovery has facilitated the analysis of its atmosphere, which is similar to other young brown dwarfs, and has allowed for the first detailed study of its atmosphere in such a low-temperature object. The observations have also provided the first direct evidence for clouds in this brown dwarf, which could be crucial for understanding its formation and evolution.

Our study focuses on the production of various particles including pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. The rapidity distribution and transverse momentum spectra of these particles were analyzed for central collisions using the STAR detector. The results indicate an enhanced production of non-zero quickness pseudoparticles compared to proton counterparts, while kaons and protons show comparable yields. The measured yN and pT distributions for these particles closely resemble those from Xe-pe collisions at a lower energy level. Additionally, the toon-to-proton yield ratio exceeds the corresponding value in Xe-pe collisions both at the same and lower energy levels in the most central collisions. The production of particles including $\phi$ mesons is elevated in Xe-Xe collisions at a significant extent compared to the previous measurements.

We introduce two innovative formulas for calculating lattice QCD hadron structure form factors. The first employs nucleon and meson light-quark PCAC constants, while the second utilizes novel lattice QCD parton distribution function (PDF) moments and is valid for any large-B value. By applying a parton model interpretation to these moments, we obtain effective interpolation and extrapolation of lattice QCD data. This approach avoids the need for extractions of external quark masses or anomalous dimensions. Furthermore, it enables us to make an accurate large-$x$ prediction for the second moment of the nucleon's spin PDF, based solely on quark and gluon distribution at a specific scale. This outcome exemplifies the potential to leverage effective theories for utilizing lattice QCD data.

In-situ 3D printing on other celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars is being explored for building habitats using local materials. Using heat to sinter building materials, obtained from thermal decomposition of carbonates, has shown potential in other planets. Forming materials from Martian and Lunar soil through heat application has shown success in small scale experiments. Mechanical tests in a vacuum environment revealed that materials from Mars and the Moon retained their strength after heat application. Adding binding agents like silica sand improved the materials' cohesion and compressive strength. Computational models were developed to analyze stress in the materials and identify patterns of failure.

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a liquid layer on a cylindrical fiber is analyzed with considerations for both slippery walls and viscous flow within the liquid. An initial assumption is that the liquid's Reynolds number is negligible. An analytical model is developed based on the assumption that the liquid layer is thin and is capable of predicting how it evolves over time due to instability breakdown. This prediction is validated through comparisons with numerical simulations and experimental results for very long, extremely thin drops formed on a fiber. As the liquid grows in length, the distance between consecutive instabilities is proportional to the cube of the liquid layer's thickness and the first critical wavelength is directly related to the cube of the thickness and the kinematic viscosity of the liquid. These findings agree with the theoretical and experimental data for a range of liquid types, including formvar and olive oil.

We have developed an accurate method for estimating the H2 molecular outflow rate in molecular gas-powered star-forming regions. The technique uses the continuum emission and hydrogen recombination lines, particularly the H-n7 spectrum, to determine the outflow rate through an extended equation based on the case B approximation of star formation. By utilizing the spectral energy distribution, the H2 and H-n7 emission rates are calculated and compared to those derived from other tracers like N2S+ and PAH-6, allowing for an accurate assessment of dust star formation efficiency. Furthermore, we have identified a correlation between the H-n7 and N2S+ emission rates, providing a reliable indicator for detecting obscured star-forming regions.

This two-part study examines the Borel subalgebra of the special linear Lie algebra, and its relationship with an associated quantum group. The branch rules of the subalgebra's highest weight representations are analyzed, particularly those related to the full Lie algebra, which serve as the foundation for classifying regional modules within the category. A key concept involves establishing an equivalence between quantum subalgebra modules and a sheaf action on a stack, enabling a description of the category's objects and morphisms on the stack level.

In recent years, score-based methods like diffusion models have gained popularity for generating high-quality data, largely due to their well-established theoretical framework. However, extending score-based modeling to non-Gaussian distributions, such as those found in real-world data, poses significant challenges. This paper presents a theoretical approach to extending score-based methods to universal distributions using the canonical diffusion process on a universal manifold. The proposed method involves three key steps: (1) mapping data to a manifold using a neural network, (2) computing score functions for conditional Gaussian distributions, and (3) solving the reverse process to sample from the original data distribution. The authors conduct extensive experiments on various datasets and demonstrate the method's effectiveness in realistic scenarios.

In the current educational setting, evaluating students' mathematical problem-solving skills is an essential component.
However, there is a significant limitation in how students write their answers - they use paper and pen, which makes it difficult to scan and interpret the complex equations they write by hand.
Another major challenge arises from the ambiguous nature of handwritten equations, as many equations written by students are structurally ambiguous, making them difficult to understand if not written in a standard format.
To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative system that leverages the movements of students writing equations, captured by a sensor, to accurately identify the underlying mathematical expression.
Our system successfully distinguishes between written equations and accurately identifies the expression even in the case of ambiguous equations, by utilizing a specially designed hierarchical temporal convolutional transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model.
We have also created a comprehensive dataset consisting of equations annotated with their mathematical meaning, which can be used to train and evaluate our approach.
Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in overcoming the challenges of handwritten equation recognition.

For speech synthesis, generating the total spoken duration is a crucial step that must be completed before any words can be produced. Although this research area has received significant attention, a comprehensive solution for total spoken duration estimation has yet to be found. The main challenge lies in accurately predicting the total spoken duration, as it depends on combining the speech lengths of individual utterances, which are often approximated using Gaussian models. These estimations can lead to inaccurate results, particularly for non-syllabic speech lengths. To address this limitation, this research introduces a novel median-based approach for synthesizing speech lengths, which overcomes the shortcomings of previous methods and achieves more accurate results. The proposed method also considers the inherent non-Gaussian characteristics of speech data. In addition to speech and linguistic features, the research also investigates the effect of speaker characteristics on total spoken duration, ultimately yielding more accurate and speaker-specific estimations. The results show that this research significantly outperforms the existing state-of-the-art techniques in estimating speech lengths, with a 19% to 35% improvement.

Environmental scientists and managers often rely on species occurrence data to create integrated models that account for the simultaneous observation of multiple species. A common observation issue in ecological studies is "pseudo-absence," where a species is recorded as absent simply because it wasn't seen during the survey. These pseudo-absences typically follow a different distribution than true absences, which can result in biased parameter estimates. In this study, two new statistical models are introduced to handle this challenge: one for observing individual species and another for observing groups of species. These models incorporate different thresholds for detection and pseudo-absence, which can be estimated using a hierarchical Bayesian approach. We compare our models to an existing method and assess their performance through extensive simulations. Additionally, the new methods are applied to real-world datasets from amphibian surveys to demonstrate their practical value. These and other integrated models are implemented in a user-friendly R package called spHabitat, which can be obtained from CRAN.

Skin lesions, the most prevalent skin condition, require careful monitoring
for early detection of malignant lesions. This monitoring is typically
conducted by healthcare professionals who analyze various factors such as a
patient's history and the physical characteristics of the skin lesion.
However, detecting early-stage skin lesions can be challenging due to their
visual similarity to benign lesions. A typical examination involves a
healthcare professional reviewing multiple cases and assessing the risk of
malignancy for each lesion, with an average analysis time of around 10 minutes.
A key factor in this process is accurately identifying the color and shape
characteristics of the skin lesion, which can be challenging for both
patients and healthcare professionals. This is where The Skincare initiative
enters The Skincare initiative, a profound interactive learning system for
skin lesion diagnosis, uses advanced computer vision techniques to analyze
skin lesion images and provide real-time diagnostic support to healthcare
professionals. By combining these techniques, The Skincare initiative can
extract meaningful insights from skin lesion images, such as color and shape
characteristics, and use this information to make an informed diagnosis.
This system also allows healthcare professionals to provide feedback on the
diagnostic suggestions made by The Skincare initiative, further enhancing its
diagnostic capabilities. As a result, The Skincare initiative has the potential
to improve skin lesion diagnosis, ultimately leading to better patient
outcomes.

Type Ia supernovae have long been regarded as reliable indicators for measuring cosmic expansion, thanks to their uniform brightness. Although researchers have made significant advancements in this field thanks to enhanced data analysis techniques, the potential of utilizing a machine learning approach to predict future supernovae remains largely unexplored. Our investigation centers on the application of a novel, probabilistic autoencoder technique to process time-series data from supernovae explosions, ultimately enabling more accurate predictions of key parameters, including peak brightness, K. A systematic comparison with existing methods, including principal component analysis, confirms the effectiveness of our proposed approach, including a comprehensive evaluation of its capabilities in predicting peak brightness, duration, and other critical parameters. Our research demonstrates the potential of employing unsupervised machine learning methods to investigate important aspects of supernovae explosions.

This study focuses on the galaxy HS 2215+4229, which exhibits both dust and free-free emission. By combining data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we have determined that the Hubble images are consistent with a combination of a bright central galaxy and multiple fainter arcs. Furthermore, our Hubble and Chandra observations reveal that HS 2115+4229 is not a quasar due to the lack of significant central X-ray emission. Instead, the observed free-free emission supports the hypothesis that HS 2215+4229 is a galaxy undergoing intense star formation. Notably, HS 2215+4229 appears to be consistent with other similarly magnified galaxies, suggesting that it may host star formation occurring within a galaxy spiral arm. Moreover, our data indicates that the HS 2215+4229 galaxy may possess a low-mass black hole with a mass of approximately 10 to 100 times that of our own black hole.

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are significantly influenced by their internal particle concentration, leading to diverse outcomes based on the number of particles involved. To investigate plume incorporation rates in high particle-count scenarios, our research employs high-speed stereo-DIC technology to analyze both empty and particle-filled vertical plumes. Our results indicate that during early-stage development, the presence of particles causes turbulent plumes to narrow, yet this effect diminishes over time as the plumes containing particles begin fall behind those that are empty. To account for decreased incorporation rates in scenarios with a high particle count, a theoretical model has been developed that relates specific energy transfer to particles with the corresponding extension of the viscous subrange in the turbulent cascade. This increase in energy transfer to particles may lead to enhanced coagulation and the formation of larger particle clusters that interfere with plume expansion. To further investigate turbulent plume dynamics, our research utilizes a self-sustaining flow system that mimics the formation of natural plumes, along with both numerical simulations and experimental observations. These studies reveal an early-stage stage where the presence of particles causes plumes to grow at an accelerated rate, yet beyond a critical particle count, the presence of particles significantly inhibits plume expansion, resulting in decreased incorporation rates.

Over the last two decades, understanding how epidemics spread has led researchers to apply network theory, where relationships are depicted as connections between individuals and infected to new individuals based on established networks. However, many modern social interactions occur within the same small groups, an aspect that traditional networks do not fully capture. Researchers have begun using hypergraphs, which can represent both one-on-one and many-to-many interactions. In this context, we develop a method to analyze the threshold for infection spread in a type of hypergraph. By applying many-to-many interactions to various scenarios, we demonstrate that the general threshold depends crucially on a property called the effective degree, which combines the size of each interaction and the degree of each individual.

Recent experimental findings in single-crystal research have shown that a two-dimensional (2D) crystal of chromium iodide, arranged in a specific orientation, exhibits ferromagnetic properties in addition to its well-known antiferromagnetic behavior. This characteristic, which is present only in a single layer of the material, appears to spontaneously switch between directional magnetization when individual layers are brought together. This spontaneous directional magnetization, which is present in addition to the material's ferromagnetic properties, could be a manifestation of a magnetic effect known as "Rashba" interaction, which is typically associated with certain types of semiconductors. This phenomenon, which is present in addition to the material's ferromagnetic properties, has been observed in an experimental setting, which is consistent with predictions made through the application of a type of theoretical modeling known as "Density Functional Theory" (DFT). This Theoretical modeling, which is applied to the material, has allowed for the identification of key factors that govern the material's magnetic behavior, which is, in turn, influenced by the material's unique electronic structure, which is, in turn, influenced by the material's geometric arrangement of its constituent atoms.
